title: Number System
subtitle: Classification, Divisibility, Factors, Remainders, Cyclicity & More

readingSections.title: The Number Family (Classification)
readingSections.quickSummary: Every exam number question starts with knowing which family a number belongs to: natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational, real, complex.
content: Numbers are grouped into nested families. Each family adds new members, and the key to classification questions is knowing exactly which family a given number falls into — and which it does NOT.
The nesting from inside out:
$$\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$$

subsections.title: Natural numbers
content: Counting numbers starting from 1: $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots$
There is no largest natural number — the set is infinite. Note that $0$ is NOT a natural number (it is the first whole number).

subsections.title: Whole numbers
content: Natural numbers plus zero: $0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
The only new member compared to naturals is $0$.

example.prompt: Which of these is a whole number but not a natural number?
steps: $0$ is a whole number and is not natural.
Negative numbers are integers, not whole numbers.

subsections.title: Integers
content: Whole numbers plus their negatives: $\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
Integers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, but NOT under division (e.g. $1 \div 2$ is not an integer).

subsections.title: Rational and irrational numbers
content: Rational: any number expressible as $\frac{p}{q}$ with integers $p, q$ and $q \neq 0$. Terminating decimals ($0.5$) and repeating decimals ($0.\overline{3}$) are rational.
Irrational: cannot be written as a fraction — non-terminating, non-repeating decimals. Examples: $\sqrt{2}, \pi, e$.
Key fact: between any two rationals there is another rational (and an irrational too) — the rationals are dense, but so are the irrationals.

example.prompt: Which of the following is irrational? $\frac{3}{4},\ \sqrt{81},\ \sqrt{2},\ 2.5$
steps: $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a fraction — irrational.

subsections.title: Real and complex numbers
content: Real = rational $\cup$ irrational — everything on the number line.
Complex = $a + bi$ where $i = \sqrt{-1}$. Every real number is complex with $b = 0$.
Numbers with no real square root like $\sqrt{-4}$ live in the complex family.

subsections.title: Place value and face value
content: Face value of a digit is the digit itself. Place value is digit $\times$ its positional power of 10.
In $4567$: the place value of $5$ is $5 \times 100 = 500$; its face value is $5$.

example.prompt: In the number $82931$, what is the difference between the place values of the digit $2$ and the digit $3$?
steps: Digit $2$ is in the thousands place: place value $= 2 \times 1000 = 2000$.
Digit $3$ is in the tens place: place value $= 3 \times 10 = 30$.

tricks: Memorize one chain: natural ⊂ whole ⊂ integer ⊂ rational ⊂ real ⊂ complex.
0 and negative numbers are the usual 'trick' answers — check the boundary.
A square root of a perfect square ($\sqrt{81}$) is rational; a square root of a non-perfect square ($\sqrt{2}$) is irrational.
Every integer is rational (write it as $\frac{n}{1}$), but not every rational is an integer.
patterns: 'Which is NOT ...?' questions test the boundary members of one family.
If options mix fractions, roots and decimals, test each option against the definition, don't guess by look.
Repeating decimal (e.g. $0.\overline{12}$) = rational; non-repeating infinite decimal = irrational.

pyqPatterns.question: Which is the smallest whole number? (Options: 0, 1, -1, none)
pyqPatterns.approach: Whole numbers start at 0 — pick 0. Only integers include negatives.

pyqPatterns.question: How many rational numbers lie between 3 and 4?
pyqPatterns.approach: Infinitely many — rationals are dense. Never pick a finite count.

quickRevision: Natural: 1,2,3,...  |  Whole: add 0  |  Integer: add negatives
Rational = p/q form or terminating/repeating decimal
Real = rational + irrational; every real is complex (b=0)
readingSections.companyNote: Classification questions appear in nearly every placement test as the first 'easy' question — do not lose it.

readingSections.title: Primes & Composites — The Building Blocks
readingSections.quickSummary: A prime has exactly 2 factors. Every composite is a product of primes. Mastering primality tests and the prime checklist solves a huge share of number-system questions.
content: Think of primes as the atoms of the number world: every composite number is built from primes, and every question about factors, divisibility or LCM/HCF ultimately runs on primes.
Prime: a natural number $> 1$ with exactly two factors — $1$ and itself. Composite: a natural number $> 1$ with more than two factors.

subsections.title: The prime checklist
content: $2$ is the smallest prime and the ONLY even prime — every other even number is composite.
The first ten primes:
$1$ is neither prime nor composite. $0$ is neither.

example.prompt: Which is the only even prime number?
steps: Every even number $> 2$ is divisible by $2$, so it has more than two factors.
Only $2$ itself escapes — its factors are $1$ and $2$.

subsections.title: Checking if a number is prime
content: Step 1: Find $\sqrt{n}$.
Step 2: Divide $n$ by each prime $\leq \sqrt{n}$.
Step 3: If none divides it, $n$ is prime.

steps: $97$ is odd; digit sum $9+7=16$ not divisible by $3$; doesn't end in $5$; $97 \div 7 = 13$ remainder $6$.
No prime divides $97$, so it is prime.

subsections.title: Twin primes and co-primes
content: Twin primes: primes differing by 2, like $(3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19)$.
Co-prime (relatively prime): two numbers whose HCF is 1. They need not be prime: $(8, 15)$ is co-prime.
Any two consecutive numbers are always co-prime, e.g. $(14, 15)$.
Consecutive odd numbers differ by 2 and are co-prime.

steps: $(14,21)$: $14$ and $21$ share factor $7$ — HCF is $7$, NOT co-prime.

subsections.title: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
content: Every composite number has ONE unique prime factorisation (up to ordering).
This is why prime factorisation is the universal tool: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ is the only way to break 360 into primes.

tricks: Quick filters in order: even? ends in 5? digit sum divisible by 3? then check 7, 11, 13.
For 'how many primes between a and b', list the candidates after applying the 2/3/5 filters — rarely need to test all.
2 and 3 are the only consecutive primes. (2,3) is the only twin-prime pair involving 2.
patterns: 'Which is NOT a prime' — test 2 (even), digit sum 3, ends in 5 first.
Product/sum of primes questions: remember 2 is the only even prime — sum of two primes is odd unless one of them is 2.
If two primes differ by 2 (twins), and the middle number is between them — the middle is always even (and composite if > 4).

pyqPatterns.question: How many prime numbers exist between 1 and 100?
pyqPatterns.approach: 25 primes. Known list — memorize rather than sieve in exam.

pyqPatterns.question: Product of the first 25 primes is even or odd?
pyqPatterns.approach: Contains 2, so the product is even — and divisible by every prime on the list.

quickRevision: Prime = exactly 2 factors; smallest is 2; only even prime is 2
Twin primes differ by 2; co-prime = HCF 1 (need not be prime)
readingSections.companyNote: Primality checks up to 100 (and 100–200) are direct exam favourites — TCS, Infosys and Cognizant have all repeated them.

readingSections.title: Divisibility Rules
readingSections.quickSummary: Divisibility rules replace long division with digit tricks. Master 2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11 first; 7 and 13 have standard shortcuts that appear regularly.
content: A number $N$ is divisible by $d$ if $N \div d$ leaves remainder 0. Rules let you check this from the digits alone. The two workhorses: last-digit rules (2,4,5,8,10) and sum-of-digits rules (3,9).

subsections.title: Rules by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11
content: $$2: \text{ last digit even} \qquad 5: \text{ last digit } 0 \text{ or } 5 \qquad 10: \text{ last digit } 0$$
$$3: \text{ sum of digits divisible by } 3 \qquad 9: \text{ sum of digits divisible by } 9$$
$$4: \text{ last two digits divisible by } 4 \qquad 8: \text{ last three digits divisible by } 8$$
$$6: \text{ divisible by both } 2 \text{ and } 3$$
$$11: \text{ (sum of digits in odd places)} - \text{(sum in even places)} \text{ is } 0, 11, \text{ or multiple of } 11$$

steps: Divisible by 9 requires digit sum divisible by 9.
None of $12, 13, 15$ is divisible by $9$ — so NONE of them is divisible by 9.

subsections.title: Rule for 7 (shortcut)
content: Double the last digit, subtract from the rest, repeat:
$$N \to \lfloor N/10 \rfloor - 2 \times \text{(last digit)}$$
If the result is $0$ or divisible by $7$, $N$ is divisible by $7$.

subsections.title: Rule for 11 in detail
content: From the RIGHT, mark digits alternately +, −, +, − … then add them with signs. Or from the left — the rule is the same, sign flips are consistent.
$22$ is a multiple of $11$ — so $918082$ is divisible by $11$.

subsections.title: Composite rules: build from factors
content: Divisible by $ab$ (with co-prime $a, b$) iff divisible by both $a$ and $b$: $6 = 2 \times 3$, $12 = 3 \times 4$, $15 = 3 \times 5$, $18 = 2 \times 9$.
Caveat: $a, b$ must be co-prime — $36 = 4 \times 9$ works, but you cannot use $36 = 6 \times 6$ as a test.

steps: $312$: digit sum $6$ (div by 3); last two digits $12$ (div by 4).
$322$: last two digits $22$ not div by 4.

tricks: 3 and 9 use the SAME digit-sum idea — if divisible by 9 then by 3, never the reverse.
For 6: test 2 first (cheaper), then 3.
For 7, 11, 13 combined: $7 \times 11 \times 13 = 1001$. Any number of form $abcabc$ (e.g. $217217$) is divisible by 7, 11 and 13.
When a question asks 'divisible by 8', only the last three digits matter — ignore everything to the left.
Digit sum trick for remainder: remainder of $N \div 9$ equals digit-sum of $N$ mod 9 (casting out nines).
patterns: 'Replace * in 23*4 to make divisible by 9' — solve from the digit-sum equation.
'Smallest number to add/subtract to make divisible by 9' — use remainder from digit sum.
Tests like 12, 15, 18 decompose into co-prime pairs — always decompose, never test directly.

pyqPatterns.question: If 451*603 (star = one digit) is divisible by 9, what digit replaces *?
pyqPatterns.approach: Digit sum $4+5+1+*+6+0+3 = 19+*$ must be divisible by 9 → $* = 8$. (Several published answers say 7 — verified: 27 is the only multiple in range, and $19+8=27$.)

pyqPatterns.question: What least number should be added to 6709 to make it divisible by 9?
pyqPatterns.approach: Digit sum $6+7+0+9 = 22$; next multiple of 9 is 27; add $27-22 = 5$.

quickRevision: 2/5/10: last digit | 4: last two | 8: last three
11: alternate-sum difference is 0 or multiple of 11
readingSections.companyNote: Digit-replacement divisibility questions are a certified TCS NQT repeat — always solve via digit sum.

readingSections.title: HCF & LCM
readingSections.quickSummary: HCF is the largest common divisor; LCM is the smallest common multiple. Their product identity — HCF × LCM = product of the numbers — is the single most tested relation.
content: HCF (GCD): the largest number that divides all given numbers. LCM: the smallest number divisible by all given numbers.
The master identity for two numbers $a, b$:
$$HCF(a,b) \times LCM(a,b) = a \times b$$

subsections.title: HCF by prime factorisation
content: HCF = product of common prime factors with the SMALLEST exponent.
For $24 = 2^3 \times 3$ and $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$:

subsections.title: LCM by prime factorisation
content: LCM = product of ALL prime factors with the LARGEST exponent.
For $24$ and $36$:

example.prompt: Find HCF and LCM of 40 and 56.

subsections.title: LCM of fractions
content: $$LCM\left(\frac{a}{b}, \frac{c}{d}\right) = \frac{LCM(a, c)}{HCF(b, d)}$$
$$HCF\left(\frac{a}{b}, \frac{c}{d}\right) = \frac{HCF(a, c)}{LCM(b, d)}$$

subsections.title: Co-prime and product relations
content: For co-prime numbers, HCF = 1 and LCM = product.
If HCF of two numbers is $h$ and ratio is $a : b$ (with $a, b$ co-prime), the numbers are $ah$ and $bh$.
Least number exactly divisible by 2,3,4,5,6 = LCM(2,3,4,5,6) = 60.

example.prompt: Two numbers are in ratio 3:5 and their HCF is 12. Find the numbers.

subsections.title: n numbers: pairwise identity caveat
content: For THREE or more numbers, HCF × LCM ≠ product — the identity holds only for two numbers.
$$HCF \text{ of } (a, b, c) \times LCM(a, b, c) \neq a \times b \times c \quad \text{(in general)}$$
This is a classic trap: the two-number identity gets misapplied.

tricks: HCF × LCM = a × b — use it to find any one unknown from the other three.
Co-prime numbers: HCF = 1, LCM = product.
HCF of fractions: HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators (swap!).
Greatest number dividing all of them = HCF; smallest number divisible by all = LCM.
HCF of consecutive numbers = 1; LCM of consecutive numbers = their product (they are co-prime).
patterns: Ratio + HCF questions: numbers = ratio × HCF.
'Least number divisible by a,b,c' = LCM.
'Greatest number that divides a,b,c leaving same remainder r' = HCF(a−r, b−r, c−r) or HCF(a,b,c) if remainder 0.
Bell-ringing / traffic-light / circular-track questions = LCM of the intervals.

pyqPatterns.question: HCF of two numbers is 12 and their product is 2880. Find LCM.
Find the largest number which divides 245 and 1029 leaving remainder 5 in each case.

quickRevision: HCF × LCM = a × b (two numbers only!)
readingSections.companyNote: The product identity and ratio+HCF questions appear in TCS, Infosys and Cognizant with very high frequency.

readingSections.title: Cyclicity & Unit Digit Patterns
readingSections.quickSummary: The unit digit of powers repeats in cycles. Find the cycle length, divide the exponent by it, and read the answer from the remainder — no big powers needed.
content: The unit digit of $a^n$ depends only on the unit digit of $a$, and repeats in a fixed cycle. This turns 'unit digit of $7^{345}$' into a small division problem.

subsections.title: The four cycle families
content: Cycle 1 (always same): $0, 1, 5, 6$ — unit digit never changes: $6^n$ ends in 6 for every $n \geq 1$.
Cycle 2: $4^n$ alternates $4, 6$; $9^n$ alternates $9, 1$.
Cycle 4: $2, 3, 7, 8$ repeat every 4 powers.

subsections.title: The division method
content: Cycle length $c$; compute $n \bmod c$; if remainder is 0, use the $c$-th (last) power in the cycle.
For $7^{345}$: cycle of 7 is $7, 9, 3, 1$ (length 4).
$$345 \bmod 4 = 1 \Rightarrow \text{ first power } \Rightarrow 7$$

subsections.title: Products and sums of unit digits
content: Unit digit of a product = unit digit of (unit digits of factors).
$$\text{unit}(8314 \times 8415) = \text{unit}(4 \times 5) = \text{unit}(20) = 0$$
Same idea for sums and differences.

subsections.title: Negative exponents? No — but negative bases
content: If base is negative, use the unit digit of |base| and fix the sign: $(-7)^n$ has unit digit of $7^n$, sign depends on parity of $n$.
When the base itself ends in 0 or 1 (like $2026^{2026}$), answer is immediately 6 or 1 — no cycle needed.

tricks: 0, 1, 5, 6: any power → same unit digit. 4/9: alternate. 2/3/7/8: cycle of 4.
If exponent is a multiple of 4, unit digit is the 4th member: 2→6, 3→1, 7→1, 8→6.
For a number ending in digit d raised to n, ONLY d matters — strip the rest.
Unit digit of (a × b × c) = unit digit of (unit(a) × unit(b) × unit(c)).
patterns: Huge exponents with bases ending in 2/3/7/8 → exponent mod 4.
Exponents with bases ending 4/9 → parity of exponent (mod 2).
Bases ending 0/1/5/6 → trivial, answer is the base's last digit.
Product/sum of powers → solve each factor's unit digit, then combine.
quickRevision: Exponent mod cycle-length; remainder 0 → last member
readingSections.companyNote: Cyclicity is a guaranteed question in TCS NQT, Infosys and Wipro. One cycle table = all variants.

readingSections.title: Remainders — Wilson, Euler, Fermat & CRT
readingSections.quickSummary: Big-power remainders are solved with modular shortcuts: binomial splitting for 1±mod patterns, Fermat for prime moduli, Wilson for factorials, Euler for general moduli, and CRT to combine congruences.
content: Remainder questions with enormous exponents are impossible by brute force — they are solved by modular arithmetic. The four tools cover the exam universe of remainder problems.

subsections.title: Binomial splitting: the workhorse
content: Split the base as (multiple of modulus ± 1) or (multiple ± small k), then expand: only the last term survives.
$$\text{Rem}\left(\frac{8^{103}}{7}\right) = \text{Rem}\left(\frac{(7+1)^{103}}{7}\right) = \text{Rem}\left(\frac{1^{103}}{7}\right) = 1$$

example.prompt: Find the remainder when $17^{200}$ is divided by 18.

subsections.title: Fermat's little theorem
content: If $p$ is prime and $p \nmid a$:
$$a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$$
Reduce the exponent by multiples of $p-1$ first, then handle the remainder.

example.prompt: Find the remainder when $5^{100}$ is divided by 13.

subsections.title: Euler's totient extension
content: For any modulus $m$ with $\gcd(a, m) = 1$:
$$a^{\varphi(m)} \equiv 1 \pmod m, \qquad \varphi(m) = m\prod_{p \mid m}\left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)$$

example.prompt: Find the remainder when $3^{100}$ is divided by 10 using Euler's theorem.

subsections.title: Wilson's theorem
content: For prime $p$:
$$(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$$
Most exam versions ask for remainder of $(p-1)!$ or a rearranged factorial product mod a small prime.

example.prompt: Find the remainder when $6!$ is divided by 7.

subsections.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)
content: Combine congruences with pairwise co-prime moduli:
$$x \equiv a_1 \pmod{m_1}, \quad x \equiv a_2 \pmod{m_2}, \quad m = m_1 m_2$$
Find $M_1 = m/m_1$, its inverse mod $m_1$, then $x = \sum a_i M_i M_i^{-1} \bmod m$.

subsections.title: Remainder of a number by 9 (casting out nines)
content: Remainder of $N \div 9$ = digit-sum of $N$ reduced mod 9 (0 → 9).

tricks: Try binomial split (base = multiple of modulus ± k) FIRST — it solves most problems in one line.
If modulus is prime and exponent ≥ modulus − 1, Fermat applies: reduce exponent mod (p−1).
Remainder of N ÷ 9 = digit sum mod 9; remainder of N ÷ 11 = alternate-sum difference mod 11.
For (a + b) mod m with huge a: compute a mod m, then add.
When a and m share a factor, Fermat/Euler do NOT apply — factor out the common divisor first.
patterns: Base ≡ ±1 mod m → answer ±1 by parity of exponent.
Exponent huge + prime modulus → exponent mod (p−1) via Fermat.
Two simultaneous congruences with co-prime moduli → CRT (or just list from the bigger modulus).
Factorial mod prime p → Wilson.
Remainder by 9/11 → digit tricks, not long division.

pyqPatterns.question: A number divided by 56 leaves remainder 29. What is the remainder when divided by 8?
pyqPatterns.approach: $29 \bmod 8 = 5$ — the quotient part is divisible by 8, only the remainder matters.

readingSections.companyNote: Fermat- and binomial-based remainders are the hardest routinely-asked number-system questions in TCS NQT — worth mastering fully.

formulas.title: Sum of First n Natural Numbers
formulas.explanation: The sum of the first $n$ natural numbers $1+2+3+\cdots+n$ equals $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. This is derived from pairing first and last terms: $(1+n)+(2+(n-1))+\cdots$
formulas.whenToUse: Any question summing $1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ or a consecutive range 1 to n.
formulas.memoryTip: n(n+1) over 2 — 'nn plus one, cut in two'.
formulas.commonMistake: Do NOT use n/2×… on the last term: for 1..n the sum is always n(n+1)/2. For a range a..b, subtract: S(b) − S(a−1).

formulas.title: Sum of First n Odd Numbers
formulas.explanation: The sum of the first $n$ odd numbers $1+3+5+\cdots+(2n-1)$ equals $n^2$.
formulas.whenToUse: Sum of odd numbers 1,3,5,… up to n terms, or 1..n where n is odd.
formulas.memoryTip: Sum of first n odds = n². The nth odd number is 2n−1.
formulas.commonMistake: Using the odd count as (last+1)/2 wrongly when the sequence does not start at 1.

formulas.title: Sum of First n Even Numbers
formulas.explanation: The sum of the first $n$ even numbers $2+4+6+\cdots+2n$ equals $n(n+1) = n^2 + n$.
formulas.whenToUse: Sum of even numbers 2,4,6,… up to n terms.
formulas.memoryTip: Sum of first n evens = n(n+1). The nth even number is 2n.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing the count n with the last term: for evens up to 100, n = 50, not 100.

formulas.title: Sum of Squares of First n Natural Numbers
formulas.memoryTip: n(n+1)(2n+1) over 6 — 'two friends in the middle'.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the (2n+1) factor, or using the natural-sum formula.

formulas.title: Sum of Cubes of First n Natural Numbers
formulas.explanation: The sum $1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 + \cdots + n^3 = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$. This is the square of the sum of natural numbers.
formulas.memoryTip: Sum of cubes = (sum of numbers)² — the beautiful identity.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing n²(n+1)²/4 as n(n+1)²/4 — keep BOTH squares.

formulas.title: HCF × LCM = Product of Two Numbers
formulas.explanation: For any two positive integers $a$ and $b$, the product of the numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM.

example.prompt: Product of two numbers is 288, HCF is 12. Find LCM.

formulas.whenToUse: Whenever two numbers, their HCF and their LCM appear — find the fourth from any three.
formulas.memoryTip: h times l equals a times b — one equation, four unknowns.
formulas.commonMistake: Applying it to 3+ numbers — it fails there.

formulas.title: Number of Factors (Divisors)
formulas.explanation: If $N = a^{p_1} \times b^{p_2} \times c^{p_3} \times \cdots$ where $a,b,c$ are primes, then the number of factors is the product of $(\text{exponent}+1)$ for each prime.
formulas.whenToUse: Counting total factors of a number: factorise, add 1 to each exponent, multiply.
formulas.memoryTip: $$N = p^a q^b r^c \Rightarrow \text{factors} = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$$
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the +1, or factorising incompletely (e.g. missing $37$ in $888888$).

formulas.title: Sum of Factors
formulas.explanation: The sum of all factors uses the geometric series formula for each prime factor. For $N = a^p$, the sum of its powers $1+a+\cdots+a^p = \frac{a^{p+1}-1}{a-1}$.
formulas.whenToUse: Sum of all divisors of a number.
formulas.memoryTip: Product of geometric sums: $\frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p-1}$ for each prime power.
formulas.commonMistake: Summing the divisors by hand for large numbers; or using (a+1) instead of the geometric series.

formulas.title: Fermat's Little Theorem
formulas.explanation: If $p$ is a prime number and $a$ is not divisible by $p$, then $a^{p-1}$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $p$. This is crucial for solving large exponent remainder problems.
formulas.whenToUse: Remainder of $a^n \bmod p$ with prime $p$ and $p \nmid a$: reduce exponent mod $p-1$.
formulas.memoryTip: For prime p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Exponent modulo p−1.
formulas.commonMistake: Using it when p and a share a factor — it breaks. Reduce the exponent correctly.

formulas.title: Euler's Totient Theorem
formulas.explanation: If $\gcd(a,n) = 1$, then $a^{\phi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ where $\phi(n) = n\prod_{p|n}\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)$. This generalizes Fermat's theorem.
formulas.whenToUse: Remainder of $a^n \bmod m$ when $m$ is composite but $\gcd(a,m)=1$.
formulas.memoryTip: φ(m) = m·Π(1−1/p) over distinct primes of m; then a^φ ≡ 1 (mod m).
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the 1−1/p factors or using distinct primes instead of prime powers.

formulas.title: Unit Digit Cycles
formulas.formula: \text{Unit digit of } a^n \text{ repeats every } k \text{ powers}
formulas.explanation: The unit digit follows a cycle: 0,1,5,6 have $k=1$; 4,9 have $k=2$; 2,3,7,8 have $k=4$. Algorithm: $\text{unit}(a^n) = \text{cycle}[n \bmod k]$ where index $0$ = last element.
formulas.whenToUse: Unit digit of $a^n$ — cycles of length 1, 2 or 4.
formulas.memoryTip: 2,3,7,8 cycle in 4; 4,9 in 2; 0,1,5,6 forever.
formulas.commonMistake: Using mod 4 when the cycle is 2 (4 and 9).

formulas.title: Trailing Zeros in n!
formulas.explanation: Trailing zeros count the number of factors of $10 = 2\times5$. Since there are always more factors of $2$ than $5$, count factors of $5$ in $n!$.
formulas.whenToUse: Count of zeros at the end of $n!$ = number of factors of 10 = count of 5s (since 2s are plentiful).
formulas.memoryTip: Keep dividing by 5, 25, 125, … and add the quotients.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting 2s instead of 5s, or stopping at n/5 without n/25, n/125…

formulas.title: Digital Root
formulas.explanation: Digital root is the repeated sum of digits until a single digit. It equals $N \bmod 9$, with $9$ representing $0$. Perfect squares can only have DR $1,4,7,9$.
formulas.whenToUse: Remainder of N ÷ 9 (with 0 mapped to 9): sum digits until a single digit.
formulas.memoryTip: Digital root of N = N mod 9 (9 instead of 0). Works for sums, products, differences — mod 9 arithmetic.
formulas.commonMistake: Mixing up 'digital root 9' with 'remainder 0'.

formulas.title: Last Two Digits
formulas.explanation: For numbers ending in 1, the last two digits follow this pattern. For numbers ending in 5: $(10a+5)^2 = 100a(a+1)+25$, so last two digits are always $25$. For other endings, use CRT with mod $4$ and mod $25$.
formulas.whenToUse: Last two digits of powers — work mod 100; cycles of length 20 for most bases, binomial for 1- and -1-ending bases.
formulas.memoryTip: For bases ending in 1: last two digits of (…1)^n = last two of (1 + n×tens part).

formulas.title: Binomial Remainder Trick
formulas.explanation: For remainder problems like $(a+1)^n \div a$, expand binomially. All terms except $1^n$ contain factor $a$, so remainder $= 1^n = 1$. More generally, $(am+b)^n \div a$ gives remainder $b^n \div a$.
formulas.whenToUse: Remainder of (km ± r)^n ÷ m — only the last binomial term survives.
formulas.memoryTip: Expand (km+r)^n; every term except r^n is divisible by m.
formulas.commonMistake: Ignoring the ± sign: (−1)^n flips with parity.

formulas.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
formulas.explanation: Given $x \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$ with $\gcd(m_i,m_j)=1$, let $M = \prod m_i$, $M_i = M/m_i$, and $y_i$ be the modular inverse of $M_i$ modulo $m_i$ (i.e., $M_i y_i \equiv 1 \pmod{m_i}$). Then the unique solution modulo $M$ is $x \equiv \sum r_i M_i y_i \pmod{M}$.
formulas.whenToUse: Smallest x satisfying several congruences with co-prime moduli.
formulas.memoryTip: List from the largest modulus and check — fast for 2 congruences in exams.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the solution must be least positive; or moduli not co-prime.

formulas.title: Product of All Factors
formulas.explanation: If $N = a^{p_1} \times b^{p_2} \times c^{p_3} \times \cdots$, then the product of all factors of $N$ equals $N$ raised to half the number of factors. If $d(N)$ is the number of factors, then product $= N^{d(N)/2}$. Factors pair up as $f \times N/f$ giving product $N$ per pair.
formulas.whenToUse: Product of all divisors of N.
formulas.memoryTip: $$\text{product} = N^{\text{(number of factors)}/2}$$
formulas.commonMistake: Using N^factors instead of N^(factors/2).

formulas.title: Odd / Even Factor Counts
formulas.explanation: If $N = 2^{p_1} \times a^{p_2} \times b^{p_3} \times \cdots$ where $a,b$ are odd primes, then: (1) Odd factors come only from the odd primes, ignoring the power of 2. (2) Even factors = Total factors - Odd factors. The number of odd factors is $(p_2+1)(p_3+1)\cdots$.

example.prompt: How many even factors does 36 have?

formulas.whenToUse: Count factors that are odd or even separately.
formulas.memoryTip: Odd factors = drop the 2-power: (b+1)(c+1)…; even factors = total − odd.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting even factors as just the 2-exponent options.

formulas.title: Making a Number a Perfect Square
formulas.formula: \text{Multiply/Divide so each prime exponent becomes even}
formulas.explanation: To make a number a perfect square: prime factorize, then for each prime with an odd exponent, multiply by that prime (to make exponent even) or divide by that prime (to remove odd power). The least number to multiply is the product of all primes with odd exponents. The least number to divide is the product of all primes with odd exponents (removing one power of each).

example.prompt: Least number to multiply 180 by to make it a perfect square?

formulas.whenToUse: Least multiplier/divisor to turn N into a perfect square.
formulas.memoryTip: Every prime exponent must become even — multiply by the odd-exponent primes.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by the whole square-root instead of the missing factor.

formulas.title: Ways to Write N as Product of Two Factors
formulas.formula: \text{Ways} = \begin{cases} \frac{d(N)}{2} & \text{if } N \text{ is not a perfect square} \\ \frac{d(N)+1}{2} & \text{if } N \text{ is a perfect square} \end{cases}
formulas.explanation: The number of ways to write $N$ as a product of two factors (order not considered, i.e., $a \times b$ and $b \times a$ count as one). Factors pair up as $f$ and $N/f$. If $N$ is a perfect square, the square root pairs with itself, giving one extra unpaired factor. Number of ordered pairs = $d(N)$ (each factor pairs with its complement).

example.prompt: In how many ways can 48 be written as a product of two co-prime factors?
steps: Co-prime split: put $2^4$ and $3$ in different boxes → $2$ ways: $1 \times 48$, $3 \times 16$.

formulas.whenToUse: Count ordered/unordered factor pairs of N.
formulas.memoryTip: Unordered pairs: ⌈factors/2⌉ for non-square; (factors+1)/2 … use ceil(factors/2) — covers both.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the (n, n) pair for perfect squares.

formulas.title: Primality Test
formulas.explanation: To check if a number $n$ is prime: (1) Check if $n \leq 1$ (not prime). (2) Check if $n$ is 2 or 3 (prime). (3) Check if $n$ is even or divisible by 3. (4) For $i = 5$ to $\sqrt{n}$, check if $n$ is divisible by $i$ or $i+2$. If none divide, $n$ is prime. Since all primes $> 3$ are of form $6k \pm 1$, we only need to check divisors of the form $6k \pm 1$.
formulas.whenToUse: Deciding if n is prime quickly.
formulas.memoryTip: Check √n with primes only. 2,3,5 filters first.
formulas.commonMistake: Testing all numbers up to n, or all numbers up to √n instead of primes only.

formulas.title: Digital Root of a Square
formulas.explanation: A perfect square can only have digital root 1, 4, 7, or 9. If a number has digital root 2, 3, 5, 6, or 8, it CANNOT be a perfect square. This is a quick elimination test. Reason: squares modulo 9 are only 0,1,4,7. Since digital root = n mod 9 (with 0 mapped to 9), the possible digital roots of squares are 1,4,7,9.

example.prompt: Can $123456$ be a perfect square? (digital root check)
steps: Squares have digital root $1,4,7,9$ — $3$ is impossible.

formulas.whenToUse: Checking if N can be a perfect square — squares have digital root 1, 4, 7 or 9.
formulas.memoryTip: Square mod 9 ∈ {0,1,4,7} (digital root 9,1,4,7). Quick reject filter.
formulas.commonMistake: Treating digital root 1 as proof of square — it is only a filter.

formulas.title: Last Two Digits of Powers of 5
formulas.formula: (10a+5)^n \text{ ends with } \begin{cases} 25 & \text{if } n \geq 2 \\ 75 & \text{if } a \text{ is odd and } n=1 \text{ or sometimes } 25 \end{cases}
formulas.explanation: For a number ending in 5: $(10a+5)^1$ ends in 25 if a is even, 75 if a is odd. $(10a+5)^2 = 100a(a+1)+25$, which always ends in 25. For $n \geq 2$, the last two digits are always 25 regardless of a. This is because the square always contributes a factor of 25, and all higher powers preserve this.
formulas.whenToUse: Last two digits of $5^n$ for n ≥ 2 — always 25.
formulas.memoryTip: 5² = 25; multiplying by 5 keeps …25 forever.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering 25 for n=1 (that's 5).

mcqs.q: What is the smallest prime number?
mcqs.exp: Step 1: By definition, a prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Step 2: 0 is not prime (undefined). 1 has only one factor (itself), so it is neither prime nor composite. Step 3: 2 has factors 1 and 2 - it is the smallest and only even prime. Step 4: Answer is 2.
